svg.text: Autonomy Removed the People, Not the Dust
What changes when the cab is empty — and the one line that does not.
CONVENTIONAL HAULAGE
AUTONOMOUS AND ELECTRIC HAULAGE
People on the haul
Who is physically present
A driver in every truck, operators on every shovel, fitters and
supervisors moving around the benches all shift.
Cabs removed entirely; crews relocated to a control room that
may be kilometres from the pit, on a 5G or 5G-A link.
Light vehicles
The flag-on-a-pole fleet
Pickups, survey utes and visitors — every one carrying a tall flag,
because a person is invisible to a truck that sits above the cab roof.
Largely withdrawn. Fewer people to carry means fewer light
vehicles, and fewer of the closest misjudgements on the ramps.
Visibility risk
Shared road, degraded view
Human eyesight, periodically reduced by dust, on roads shared
with vehicles in the 200 to 400 tonne class.
Lidar, millimetre-wave radar and camera stacks hold station in
tens of metres of visibility, in snow, dust and darkness.
Who carries the exposure
Occupational health
Silica, noise, vibration, dust and collision risk are borne by
people, continuously, for a working lifetime.
Occupational exposure falls sharply; dust becomes a maintenance,
permit and boundary compliance problem instead.
Dust generated per tonne moved
Unchanged by either technology
Tyres shear the running surface and lift the silt fraction, driven by
speed, axle load and moisture — none of which know who is driving.
Zero tailpipe particulate is a real gain, but mechanical dust is not
combustion dust. The source term stays where it was.
The second-order effect: the road loses its sensors.
A driver on a ten-hour haul cycle feels every rut and reports the plume in the mirror. An empty cab measures nothing — so an autonomous mine needs more instrumentation, not less.
